extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and design patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparation, filing, and examination of U.S. design patent applications (35 U.S.C. chapter 16) including specification, drawings, claim form, practitioner requirements, and related procedural matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis for design patents (35 U.S.C. 171)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents any new, original, and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a patent therefor; filing date is the date on which the specification as prescribed by section 112 and any required drawings are filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provisions of the patent statutes generally apply to design patents except as otherwise provided. For international design applications see 35 U.S.C. chapter 38 and MPEP Chapter 2900. The filing date rules reference compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements and required drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a design (subject matter of a design patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a design patent application, the subject matter which is claimed is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture (or portion thereof) and not the article itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design consists of the visual characteristics embodied in or applied to an article — configuration, surface ornamentation, or combination. A design is inseparable from the article to which it is applied, must be a definite, preconceived thing capable of reproduction, and cannot be a design in the abstract. Case citations (e.g., In re SurgiSil; Curver Luxembourg) emphasize that a design claim is limited to the article identified in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between design and utility patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents protect the way an article is used and works (35 U.S.C. 101), while design patents protect the way an article looks (35 U.S.C. 171).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key differences summarized include: (A) term — utility 20 years from filing vs design 15 years from grant (filed on/after May 13, 2015) (B) maintenance fees required for utility but not design (C) design applications include only a single claim (D) restriction practice mandatory in design but discretionary in utility (E) international filing routes differ (PCT for utility; Hague Agreement for design) (F) foreign priority period: 12 months (utility) vs 6 months (design) (G) provisional applications not available for design (H) RCE not available for design (I) Continued prosecution application (CPA) available for design (J) publication rules differ. Unless provided otherwise, rules for utility applications apply to design applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent practitioner bar and signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent practitioners are registered under 37 CFR 11.6(d) and have practice limited to design patent matters; design practitioners must indicate their design status adjacent to their signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handwritten signatures must include the word 'design' adjacent to the signature; S-signatures must include registration number and the word 'design' adjacent to the last forward slash. Design practitioners must meet modified technical/educational requirements (e.g., degree in industrial design, product design, architecture, applied arts, graphic design, fine/studio arts, art teacher education, or equivalents). A design practitioner cannot sign papers in utility (including provisional) or plant applications; power of attorney/customer-number rules are affected. Practitioners must provide competent representation and inform clients of practice limitations (37 CFR 11.101).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a design patent application (37 CFR 1.154)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application has essentially the elements required of a utility patent application; a drawing is an essential element and a claim in a specific form is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested order of elements: design application transmittal form; fee transmittal form; application data sheet (§ 1.76); specification; drawings or photographs; inventor's oath or declaration (§ 1.153(b)). The specification should include: preamble (name, title, brief description of nature and intended use), cross-reference to related applications, statement regarding federally sponsored research, description of the figure(s) of the drawing, feature description, and a single claim. See 37 CFR 1.154 for arrangement and MPEP ¶15.05 for framing the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and preamble requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the design must designate the particular article and the title and claim must correspond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title identifies the article by the name generally known and used by the public and may contribute to defining scope of the claim. Title may be directed to the entire article even if claim covers a portion, but the title may not be directed to less than the claimed design shown in full lines. Broad titles are permitted but may require the nature and intended use be included in the preamble. Inconsistencies between title and claim should be objected to under 37 CFR 1.153. Amendments to title must have antecedent basis in the original disclosure and may not introduce new matter (may be objected under 35 U.S.C. 132 or cause rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification content — general rule and permissible statements
rubrics_metrics.description: No description other than brief reference to the drawing is ordinarily required; however certain types of statements are permissible in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible statements include: (1) description of appearance of portions not illustrated (must be in original filing); (2) disclaimers of portions not shown as forming no part of claimed design (as originally filed for antecedent basis); (3) statement indicating purpose of broken lines (e.g., environmental structure or boundaries not part of design); (4) description of nature and intended use if not in preamble; (5) 'characteristic features' statement describing a feature considered novel or nonobvious (37 CFR 1.71(c)). The USPTO may telephone applicants at docketing to resolve nature/intended use to facilitate classification and proper search. Any added description must not introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic feature statement cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'characteristic features' statement describing a particular feature of novelty or nonobviousness may be included but does not serve as the basis for determining patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended phrasing: 'The characteristic feature of the design resides in [description].' Inclusion may later limit the claim. Patentability of a design is determined by comparison of the overall appearance with the prior art (e.g., In re Rosen; In re Leslie). The examiner will not suggest a characteristic feature statement and it is optional for applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible descriptive statements in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statements are not permitted in the specification of an issued design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impermissible statements include: (1) disclaimers directed to any portion shown in solid lines in the drawings; (2) statements describing or suggesting other embodiments not illustrated (except mirror images or shapes evident from the figure) or attempts to broaden scope beyond the drawings; (3) statements describing functional or structural matters unrelated to ornamentation. Such statements may appear in the original application to provide antecedent basis for future amendment but cannot appear in the issued specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional and structural features not considered in design cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications are concerned solely with the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture; functional and/or structural features are not considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants' emphasis on structure or function is irrelevant to design examination and falls under utility patent practice. Examiner should object to descriptions that improperly focus on function/structure in a design specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing requirements for design applications (37 CFR 1.152; §1.84)
rubrics_metrics.description: The design must be represented by a drawing that complies with § 1.84 and must contain a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate and adequate surface shading to show character or contour. Solid black surface shading is not permitted except to represent the color black or color contrast. Broken lines may show visible environmental structure but not hidden planes or surfaces not visible through opaque materials. Alternate positions of a component illustrated by full and broken lines in the same view are not permitted. Photographs and ink drawings may not be combined as formal drawings; photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must be limited to the claimed design and not disclose environmental structure. Drawings/photographs must be clear and complete; inconsistencies among views should be objected to and, if so severe that overall appearance is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim form and content for design patents (37 CFR 1.153)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application may include only a single claim, normally in formal terms to 'The ornamental design for (the article) as shown' or 'as shown and described.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim should be consistent in terminology with the title. 'And described' is added when the specification includes a proper descriptive statement. Full lines in drawings show the claimed design; broken lines serve specific purposes (e.g., environment, boundaries, stitching) and may not be used to indicate immaterial portions. The design is unitary; all portions contribute to the appearance and are material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines usage in drawings and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines may be used for certain illustrative purposes but may not be used to identify portions of the claimed design which are immaterial or unimportant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broken lines are permitted to illustrate environmental structure, boundaries, stitching, and fold lines, but are not permitted to show hidden planes or alternate positions in the same view. They cannot be used to disclaim solid-line claimed portions as 'immaterial.' Improper use may lead to objections or rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited examination (37 CFR 1.155) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for expedited examination under 37 CFR 1.155 are evaluated by the Director of Technology Center 2900 and will be initiated if the application is in condition for examination and the request is complete (including fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is recommended to file the request together with the design application for optimal processing. For international design applications, requests should be filed after publication pursuant to Hague Article 10(3). The Office will not examine an application not in condition for examination even if expedited status is requested. If a request fails to comply with requirements, applicant will be notified and may submit a renewed request; unless timely corrected, the application waits its regular turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of a design patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents resulting from applications filed on or after May 13, 2015 have a 15 year term from the date of grant; patents issued from design applications filed before that date have a 14 year term from the date of grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term is fixed and cannot be extended by reissue. See 35 U.S.C. 173 and PLTIA implementation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue practice for design patents (drawing corrections)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue application may be filed to correct an error, including corrections to the drawing, but the term of a design patent may not be extended by reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When correcting drawings in a reissue, follow 37 CFR 1.173(b)(3). Submit a copy of all drawing views, annotated marked-up drawings explaining changes, and label canceled/amended/new drawing views ('Canceled', 'Amended', 'New'). If converting solid lines to broken lines, include a statement indicating the purpose of the broken lines. The reissue specification must include figure descriptions for new views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent and copyright overlap; conditions for inclusion of a copyright notice
rubrics_metrics.description: An ornamental design may be copyrighted and also be the subject matter of a design patent; the USPTO permits inclusion of a copyright notice in a design patent application under specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: (A) copyright notice must be placed adjacent to the copyrighted material and, if on a drawing, limited in print size from 1/8 inch to 1/4 inch and placed within the sight of the drawing immediately below the figure; (B) content of notice limited to elements required by law (e.g., '© 1983 John Doe'); (C) a waiver paragraph must be included at the beginning of the specification with specific language consenting to facsimile reproduction by anyone of the patent document as it appears in USPTO records while reserving other copyright rights; (D) inclusion after Notice of Allowance permitted only if 37 CFR 1.312 criteria are satisfied. Failure to include the precise waiver language will lead to objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent and trademark overlap; trademark use in applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent and a trademark may be obtained on the same subject matter, but certain uses of trademarks in design applications are restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derogatory use of a trademark in a design application is prohibited and will result in rejection of the claim under 35 U.S.C. 171 as offensive subject matter. It is improper to use a trademark alone or coupled with 'type' in the title (e.g., 'Band-Aid type Bandage') — examiners must object and require deletion. If a trademark appears in the drawing disclosure, the specification must include a statement preceding the claim identifying the trademark material forming part of the claimed design and the name of the owner of the trademark (use form paragraph 15.76).
